title: Is Testing the Next Frontier in Ed Reform Louisiana Experiment
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler examines Louisiana's Innovative Assessment (IA), an experiment grounding reading tests in taught content rather than generic skills. Though discontinued in 2024 after only two full years, the IA showed promise: students felt less anxious, teachers shifted from isolated skills to whole-text meaning-making, and gaps between disadvantaged and affluent students narrowed. However, changing state tests requires coordination across bureaucratic silos—curriculum officials, test designers, legislatures—and the political will rarely materializes. The article argues that what gets tested gets taught, making content-aligned assessment crucial for knowledge-building reform.
points: Testing design powerfully shapes teacher practice: the IA prompted teachers to build background knowledge instead of prepping for generic skills tests.
Content-aligned tests narrow achievement gaps by allowing all students to show competence when they share relevant background knowledge.
Changing state assessment requires vision, coordination, and sustained political will—the IA died despite promise when leadership shifted.
Psychometricians' focus on reliability and comparability often overshadows questions about whether tests measure what students actually need.
quotes: To be able to make an inference, for example, you need a certain threshold of relevant background knowledge. Lots of kids lack enough background knowledge to make sense of the passages on reading tests.
Teachers made it clear that testing was the major influence shaping their instruction: 'The most important thing is whatever test we're giving, because it is how I'm judged as a teacher.'

What gets tested gets taught. If we continue to test illusory skills, that's what teachers will continue to focus on, to the continued detriment of many students.” Archived from Minding the Gap on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
